title: Treasury Management ATO via Malvertising and Vishing
text:
Threat actors target commercial banking customers using a multi-phase scheme that begins with search engine malvertising (poisoned ads impersonating bank login pages), transitions to vishing (phone-based social engineering impersonating bank staff), and culminates in unauthorized wire transfers to mule accounts. One bank documented approximately 10 attacks per day with six-to-seven-figure losses per successful incident. Cross-functional analysis using the CFPF framework traced the full kill chain and identified that mitigating the malvertising entry point eliminated successful ATOs for 8 months, saving the institution hundreds of thousands of dollars per day.

---

title: Business Email Compromise — Vendor Impersonation Wire Fraud
text: Threat actors compromise or spoof vendor email accounts, then impersonate the vendor to redirect legitimate invoice payments to actor-controlled accounts. BEC caused $2.9B+ in reported losses in 2023 per FBI IC3. The scheme exploits trust relationships between businesses and their vendors, often going undetected until the legitimate vendor inquires about unpaid invoices weeks or months later.

title: Synthetic Identity — Credit Card Bust-Out
text: Actors create fictitious identities by combining real SSNs (often belonging to children, elderly, deceased, or immigrants) with fabricated PII. They then "nurture" these synthetic identities over months or years — opening accounts, building credit history, and establishing legitimacy — before executing a coordinated "bust-out" where all available credit is maxed and the identities are abandoned. The Federal Reserve estimates synthetic identity fraud costs U.S. lenders $6B+ annually.

title: Payroll Diversion via HR Portal Compromise
text: Actors compromise employee self-service HR portals (Workday, ADP, UKG, etc.) to change direct deposit routing information, diverting paychecks to actor-controlled accounts. Often combined with email rule manipulation to suppress payroll notifications. FBI IC3 flagged this as a growing BEC variant. Low per-incident amounts ($2,000-$10,000) but high volume and often undetected for multiple pay cycles.

title: Insurance Premium Diversion via Agent Portal ATO
text: Actors compromise insurance agent portals to modify policy payment routing, diverting premium payments from policyholders to actor-controlled accounts. Alternatively, actors gain access to agent trust accounts where premiums are held before remittance to the carrier. This scheme exploits the distributed nature of insurance distribution — independent agents operate semi-autonomously with significant system access. Discovery is often delayed because policyholders believe they've paid and carriers may not flag gaps until policy cancellation for non-payment.

title: Real Estate Wire Fraud — Closing Scam
text: Actors compromise email accounts of real estate agents, title companies, attorneys, or mortgage lenders to monitor pending transactions and send fraudulent wire instructions to homebuyers at closing. The scheme exploits the time-sensitive, high-value nature of real estate closings and the expectation that wire instructions will arrive via email. FBI IC3 reports real estate BEC as one of the fastest-growing BEC subcategories, with average losses of $150,000+ (often representing a buyer's entire down payment or full purchase price).

title: Deepfake Voice Authorization for Wire Transfer
text: Actors use AI-generated voice deepfakes to impersonate executives, clients, or authorized signers during phone-based wire transfer authorization. The first publicly documented case (2019) involved a UK energy firm's CEO impersonated via deepfake voice, resulting in a $243,000 transfer. As voice cloning technology becomes more accessible and convincing, this threat path is accelerating. It specifically targets institutions that rely on voice-based dual authorization as a fraud control — turning a security measure into an attack vector.

title: SIM Swap to Cryptocurrency Exchange ATO
text: Actors social-engineer mobile carriers to transfer a victim's phone number to an actor-controlled SIM card, then use intercepted SMS-based MFA codes to take over cryptocurrency exchange accounts and drain digital assets. FBI IC3 reported $68M+ in SIM swap losses in 2021 alone, with individual losses frequently exceeding $1M for high-net-worth crypto holders. DOJ has prosecuted multiple SIM swap rings targeting crypto investors specifically.

title: Check Washing and Fraudulent Mobile Deposit
text: Actors steal checks from USPS mailboxes (using stolen arrow keys or by fishing mail from collection boxes), chemically wash the payee and amount fields, then rewrite checks to themselves or accomplices for higher amounts. Washed checks are deposited via mobile banking apps — sometimes the same stolen check is deposited multiple times across different institutions. FinCEN data shows check fraud SARs surged 200%+ from 2021-2023. Despite being a "low-tech" fraud, it's one of the fastest-growing categories due to the explosion of USPS mail theft and the ease of mobile deposit.

title: Disability Insurance Fraud via Fabricated Medical Documentation
text: Actors file fraudulent long-term or short-term disability claims using fabricated, exaggerated, or collusively obtained medical documentation. Schemes range from individual claimants exaggerating symptoms with a complicit provider to organized rings where providers generate documentation for dozens of fictitious or exaggerated claims. DOJ prosecutions reveal schemes lasting years with cumulative payouts in the millions. The long-tail nature of disability payments means a single fraudulent claim can generate $100,000+ in benefits before detection.

title: Romance Scam to Money Mule Recruitment Pipeline
text: Actors operating from organized scam compounds (primarily Southeast Asia) cultivate fake romantic or investment relationships with victims over weeks to months, then exploit the relationship to either extract money directly (romance scam) or recruit the victim as an unwitting money mule. Romance scams generated $1.1B+ in reported losses in 2023 per FBI IC3. This threat path is unique because victims are simultaneously targets AND infrastructure — recruited mules enable other fraud schemes (BEC wire fraud, check fraud, ATO). The "pig butchering" variant combines romance cultivation with fake cryptocurrency investment platforms.

title: Authorized Push Payment Fraud — Tech Support / Bank Impersonation
text: Actors contact victims impersonating bank fraud departments, tech support (Microsoft, Apple, Amazon), or government agencies (IRS, SSA), convincing them that their accounts are compromised and they must urgently transfer funds to a "safe account." Unlike traditional ATO, the victim themselves authorizes and executes the payment — making recovery extremely difficult. The UK's Payment Systems Regulator reported £460M+ in APP fraud losses in 2023. FBI IC3 reports tech support fraud as one of the highest-loss categories for victims over 60.

title: Credential Stuffing to Loyalty Point / Gift Card Account Drain
text: Actors use large-scale credential stuffing (automated testing of stolen username/password pairs from unrelated breaches) against loyalty program portals, bank rewards platforms, and gift card balance-check sites. Successful logins are used to drain stored value — transferring loyalty points to actor-controlled accounts, converting rewards to gift cards, or transferring gift card balances. Loyalty points and gift cards are attractive targets because they're less monitored than bank accounts, rarely have MFA, and can be monetized quickly through resale markets. Akamai reports billions of credential stuffing attempts per year targeting financial services.

title: Insider-Enabled Account Fraud at Financial Institution
text: Employees of financial institutions abuse their legitimate system access to commit or enable fraud — opening accounts with stolen identities, modifying customer records to facilitate unauthorized transactions, exfiltrating customer data to external fraud rings, or directly siphoning funds. The ACFE estimates that insider fraud accounts for 5% of organizational revenue globally. Financial institution insiders are particularly dangerous because they understand internal controls and know how to avoid triggering detection. Schemes often involve collusion with external actors who provide stolen identities or receive diverted funds.

title: Employment Fraud via Brand Impersonation
text: Actors impersonate legitimate employers — particularly in healthcare staffing, home care, and remote work sectors — by registering lookalike domains and creating fake job postings. Victims are "hired" through a fake onboarding process that harvests PII (SSN, banking info, government ID) for identity theft, or are charged advance fees for equipment, training, or background checks. The FBI IC3 reported $367M in employment fraud losses in 2023, with fake job scams increasing 118% year-over-year. This threat path is distinct from BEC in that the victim is the job applicant, not an employee of the impersonated company.

title: First-Party Fraud (Bust-Out)
text:
First-party fraud occurs when an individual intentionally misrepresents their identity, intent, or financial situation to obtain credit or services with no intention of repayment. This threat path focuses on the "bust-out" variation, where a customer establishes a seemingly legitimate relationship with an institution, uses the account normally for a period, and then suddenly maximizes their credit utilization before abandoning the account.

---

title: Pig Butchering (Investment Scam)
text:
"Pig Butchering" (Sha Zhu Pan) is an orchestrated, long-term social engineering scheme where perpetrators build trust with targets over weeks or months (often via dating apps or misdirected text messages) before convincing them to invest in fraudulent cryptocurrency platforms. The scam is characterized by an extended "fattening" phase where the victim sees fake returns on small initial investments, prompting them to invest massive sums before the platform disappears.

---

title: Deepfake Document Fraud
text:
Deepfake document fraud targets the Know Your Customer (KYC) and remote account onboarding processes. Criminals utilize advanced generative AI models (GANs, diffusion models) to manufacture highly realistic, synthetic identifying documents (e.g., driver's licenses, passports, utility bills) that match the details of a synthetic or stolen identity. This bypasses automated optical character recognition (OCR) and facial recognition checks used by financial institutions during self-service digital onboarding.

---

title: Business Identity Theft
text:
Business Identity Theft (or Corporate Hijacking) involves threat actors impersonating a legitimate, functioning business — typically a small to medium-sized enterprise (SME) — to open financial accounts, lines of credit, or secure loans. They exploit public corporate registration details, file fraudulent amendments with the Secretary of State, and forge documents to assume the identity of corporate officers.

---

title: Supply Chain Payment Fraud
text:
Supply Chain Payment Fraud (a variant of Vendor Impersonation / BEC) involves threat actors compromising the email account of a legitimate vendor or supplier. The actors monitor email traffic to identify upcoming large invoice payments, insert themselves into the communication chain, and provide updated, fraudulent banking instructions to the buyer. When the buyer processes the invoice, the funds are wired to a threat-actor-controlled account instead of the true vendor.

---

title: Healthcare Provider Billing Fraud
text:
Healthcare Provider Billing Fraud involves legitimate or seemingly legitimate medical providers intentionally submitting false or inflated claims to health insurance networks or government programs (like Medicare/Medicaid) for financial gain. This typically takes the form of "phantom billing" (billing for services never rendered), "upcoding" (billing for a more expensive service than provided), or "unbundling" (billing stages of a procedure separately to increase total payout).

---

title: Government Program Fraud (Unemployment/Tax)
text:
Government Program Fraud involves threat actors leveraging stolen Personally Identifiable Information (PII) to file fraudulent claims for government benefits (e.g., UI, SNAP, FEMA disaster relief) or tax refunds. The actor directs the government payout to a pre-paid debit card, a digitally opened neo-bank account, or an established mule account, depriving the legitimate citizen of their benefits and defrauding the state.

---

title: Mobile Banking Trojan / Overlay Attack
text:
Mobile Banking Trojans (primarily targeting Android environments) are sophisticated malware variants that deceive users into granting extensive device "Accessibility" permissions. Once installed, the malware monitors the foreground applications. When the user launches a targeted banking app, the malware draws a pixel-perfect "overlay" (a fake login screen) on top of the legitimate app. It captures the user's credentials and SMS MFA tokens, sending them to the threat actor, or uses an Automated Transfer System (ATS) to initiate fraudulent transactions invisibly on the victim's device.

---

title: Account-to-Account Instant Payment Fraud (Zelle / FedNow / Pix / UPI)
text:
Threat actors exploit account-to-account (A2A) instant payment rails (Zelle, FedNow, Pix, UPI, UK Faster Payments) to execute irrevocable fund transfers via social engineering, account takeover, or payment diversion schemes. The defining characteristic of this threat path is finality: real-time payment systems settle in seconds with no native chargeback mechanism, eliminating the recall window available in traditional wire and ACH channels. Attack vectors range from socially engineered authorized push payments (where the victim initiates the transfer themselves) to full account takeover on RTP-connected accounts, with monetization through layered mule account networks that rapidly disperse funds across multiple institutions within minutes of the initial transfer.

---

title: GenAI-Enhanced Authorized Push Payment Fraud — Romance Variant
text:
Threat actors leverage generative AI capabilities — including deepfake voice cloning, AI-generated profile imagery, and large language model-driven chatbots — to operate romance scam campaigns at unprecedented scale and sophistication. Unlike traditional romance scams that require skilled human operators for each victim relationship, GenAI-enhanced variants enable a single operator to maintain dozens of simultaneous romantic personas with consistent, emotionally intelligent conversations. The attack culminates in authorized push payments where the victim willingly transfers funds based on fabricated emotional bonds, with average losses of $64,000 per victim (FTC) making romance fraud the highest per-incident loss category among APP fraud types. The integration of deepfake voice and video into relationship grooming eliminates many of the traditional red flags (refusal to video call, inconsistent accents) that historically helped victims identify romance scams.

---

title: GenAI-Enhanced Authorized Push Payment Fraud — Investment Variant
text:
Threat actors deploy generative AI to create and operate fraudulent investment schemes at industrial scale, combining deepfake celebrity endorsement videos, AI-generated trading dashboards showing fabricated returns, and LLM-powered "financial advisor" personas to convince victims to invest in non-existent opportunities. This threat path represents the AI-enhanced evolution of "pig butchering" (sha zhu pan) operations where victims are "fattened" with apparent early returns before being slaughtered with total loss. The FBI IC3 reported $6.57 billion in investment fraud losses in 2024 — the single largest fraud category — with cryptocurrency investment fraud accounting for $5.8 billion of that total. Chainalysis research indicates that AI-enabled investment scams extract 4.5x more revenue per operation ($3.2M average) compared to non-AI-enhanced variants ($719K average), demonstrating the direct revenue impact of GenAI adoption by fraud operators.

---

title: Elder Financial Exploitation (Multi-Vector)
text:
Threat actors exploit adults aged 60 and older through multiple converging fraud vectors including tech support scams, romance scams, investment fraud, and government impersonation schemes. FBI IC3 reported $4.885B in losses from 101,068 complaints filed by victims 60+ in 2024, a 43% year-over-year increase, while academic estimates place the true annual figure closer to $28.3B when accounting for unreported cases. This threat path is distinguished by its multi-vector nature, the involvement of caregivers or family members in approximately 30% of cases, and the exploitation of cognitive decline, social isolation, and Power of Attorney relationships as force multipliers that enable sustained, repeated victimization.

---

title: DME Phantom Billing (Medicare Fraud)
text:
Organized fraud networks establish fraudulent Durable Medical Equipment (DME) supplier companies, obtain Medicare provider enrollment, and submit claims for medical equipment that is never delivered to patients. Operation Gold Rush and related DOJ prosecutions have documented $4.45B in fraudulent DME billing, with over 5,800 defendants prosecuted since 2007. The scheme exploits stolen Medicare beneficiary data to create phantom patient lists, registers shell companies as DME suppliers across multiple states, and bills Medicare for expensive equipment (wheelchairs, orthotic braces, CPAP machines) that beneficiaries never ordered or received. The scale of the fraud prompted CMS to impose a 6-month moratorium on new DME supplier enrollment in high-fraud geographic areas.

---

title: AI Synthetic Identity & Document Forgery
text:
Threat actors are leveraging generative AI to produce high-fidelity forged identity documents, synthetic facial images, and behavioral biometric mimicry to bypass KYC/identity verification controls at scale. Digital document forgery surpassed physical forgery in 2024, reaching 57% of all detected forgeries (a 244% increase), while AI-generated document fraud overall increased 311%. Underground services like OnlyFake and ProKYC have democratized access to convincing forged IDs, selfie-matching images, and video-based liveness check bypasses for as little as $30 per identity package. Combined with traditional synthetic identity techniques (CPN/SSN manipulation, credit farming), AI-enabled document forgery represents an evolution that threatens to overwhelm current identity verification defenses. The Federal Reserve Board estimates synthetic identity fraud generates $6B+ in annual losses to the US financial system.

---

title: E-Commerce Triangulation Fraud
text:
Triangulation fraud is a three-party e-commerce scheme where fraudsters list legitimate products on marketplace platforms (Amazon, eBay, Walmart Marketplace) at competitive prices, accept orders from unsuspecting customers, then fulfill those orders by purchasing the same products from legitimate retailers using stolen payment card data and shipping directly to the customer. The customer receives the product and is unaware that it was purchased with stolen credentials, while the legitimate retailer absorbs the chargeback when the stolen card is reported. This scheme generates an estimated $48B+ in annual marketplace fraud losses, with North American e-commerce fraud growing 207%. Organized rings operating via Telegram manage hundreds of storefronts simultaneously, creating a scalable fraud infrastructure that exploits the separation between marketplace platforms and payment processing.

---

title: Refund-as-a-Service (FTID / RaaS)
text:
Organized Refund-as-a-Service (RaaS) operations monetize retailer return policies at industrial scale by filing fraudulent refund claims on behalf of paying customers. Professional "refunders" operating through Telegram channels and underground forums charge 15-40% commission per successful refund, employing techniques such as Fake Tracking ID (FTID), Did Not Arrive (DNA), and Significantly Not As Described (SNAD) claims. With return fraud contributing to an estimated $103B in annual losses across U.S. retail, and some RaaS operations processing over 1,000 refunds per month, this threat path represents a mature, professionalized fraud-as-a-service ecosystem operating in the gray zone between first-party fraud and organized crime.

---

title: Web3 Wallet Drainer / Approval Phishing
text:
Wallet drainer operations exploit blockchain token approval mechanisms to steal cryptocurrency assets at scale. Threat actors deploy Drainer-as-a-Service (DaaS) kits — most notably Inferno Drainer (commanding 40-45% market share) — that lure victims to phishing sites impersonating legitimate Web3 projects, then trick them into signing malicious token approval or Permit/Permit2 transactions that grant the attacker unlimited access to their wallet assets. ScamSniffer reported $494M stolen via wallet drainers in 2024, and while early 2025 saw an 83% decline to approximately $84M, the DaaS model persists with new entrants replacing shuttered operations. Stolen funds are laundered through cross-chain bridges, mixers, and crypto money laundering networks (CMLNs) processing an estimated $16.1B in 2025, making attribution and recovery extremely difficult.

---

title: Ghost Student Financial Aid Botnets
text:
Organized fraud networks exploit the open-enrollment admissions model of community colleges and universities to create thousands of "ghost student" identities — synthetic or stolen identities enrolled solely to siphon federal financial aid (primarily Pell Grants via FAFSA). Bot-driven application systems submit fraudulent enrollment applications at industrial scale, with California community colleges alone flagging 31-34% of applications as potentially fraudulent. Equifax reported preventing $180M in ghost student fraud in a single year, and nationwide detection systems have prevented over $1B in fraudulent disbursements. The monetization path follows Pell Grant disbursement to student accounts, with funds immediately withdrawn or transferred before the institution can detect non-attendance, creating a systematic drain on federal education funding that simultaneously inflates enrollment figures and degrades institutional resources.

---

title: DPRK State-Sponsored IT Worker Fraud & Data Extortion
text:
The Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) operates a state-sponsored employment fraud program in which North Korean IT workers — often operating from China, Russia, and Southeast Asia — use stolen or synthetic American identities to fraudulently obtain remote employment at Western technology companies. The program generates revenue for the North Korean regime in violation of international sanctions, while simultaneously creating insider threat vectors for credential theft, source code exfiltration, and post-termination data extortion. The DOJ has documented 136+ compromised U.S. companies with $2.2M+ in direct salary revenue from a single case, while CrowdStrike has observed 304 incidents. The threat has escalated since mid-2024 from pure salary extraction to active data exfiltration and ransom demands, representing a convergence of state-sponsored espionage, employment fraud, and cyber extortion. The operation relies on organized facilitator networks spanning the U.S. and Ukraine that provide stolen identities, proxy laptop hosting at U.S. addresses, and financial laundering infrastructure.

---

title: Mule Account Velocity Pattern
text: Detects rapid inbound transfers from multiple unique senders followed by immediate outbound movement, typical of money mule activity. This rule is a shared component applicable to TP-0001, TP-0002, TP-0011, and TP-0022.

title: Infostealer Credential Dump Velocity
text: Detects rapid credential dump patterns where many unique credentials are harvested from a single host in a short timeframe. Infostealers such as RedLine, Lumma, and Vidar typically exfiltrate dozens to hundreds of stored credentials within seconds of execution, producing a burst of credential-access events from one endpoint.

title: Session Cookie Exfiltration Pattern
text: Detects session token and cookie theft patterns in log data indicative of infostealer activity. Stealers like Lumma and Raccoon target browser cookie stores to extract active session tokens, enabling session hijacking without requiring credentials. This rule monitors for suspicious access to cookie databases and exfiltration of session-bearing data.

title: Browser Credential Store Access
text: Detects unusual access to browser credential stores (Login Data, logins.json, key3.db/key4.db) by non-browser processes. Infostealers such as RedLine and Vidar systematically read these SQLite databases to extract saved usernames and passwords for banking portals and other financial services.

title: Stealer C2 Beacon Pattern
text: Detects command-and-control callback patterns typical of Malware-as-a-Service (MaaS) stealers. RedLine, Lumma, and StealC use distinctive C2 communication patterns including HTTP POST requests with base64-encoded payloads to newly registered domains, often on non-standard ports or with characteristic URI patterns.

title: Credential Testing After Dump
text: Detects rapid credential validation attempts occurring shortly after a credential dump event. After infostealers exfiltrate harvested credentials, threat actors typically run automated validation to identify which stolen credentials are still active, producing a burst of login attempts across multiple banking portals from the attacker's infrastructure.

title: Infostealer Exfiltration Archive Creation
text: Detects creation of archive files containing credential-related file patterns consistent with infostealer packaging behavior. Stealers like RedLine and Vidar collect credentials, cookies, autofill data, and crypto wallet files into a ZIP or RAR archive before exfiltrating them to the C2 server.

title: Multiple Account Access from Single Source
text: Detects multiple distinct banking accounts being accessed from a single device or IP address within a short timeframe. This pattern is consistent with an attacker using stolen credentials from an infostealer dump to sequentially access compromised accounts for reconnaissance or initial positioning before fraudulent transactions.

title: Stolen Session Token Replay
text: Detects session token replay from a different geographic location or device than the original authenticating session. When infostealers exfiltrate active session cookies, attackers import them into antidetect browsers to hijack authenticated sessions without triggering login-based detections. This rule correlates session token usage across differing geolocations and device fingerprints.

title: Autofill Data Harvesting
text: Detects form autofill data extraction patterns consistent with infostealer behavior. Stealers like RedLine and Raccoon target browser autofill databases (Web Data, formhistory.sqlite) to harvest stored PII including names, addresses, phone numbers, and payment card details that facilitate downstream fraud.

title: Crypto Wallet Seed Phrase Exfiltration
text: Detects wallet seed phrase and private key extraction attempts targeting cryptocurrency wallets. Infostealers such as RedLine, Vidar, and StealC include dedicated modules that search for wallet.dat files, seed phrase backups, and keystore directories for MetaMask, Exodus, Electrum, and other popular wallets to enable cryptocurrency theft.

title: Login Velocity Anomaly
text: Detects abnormal login attempt velocity from a single source IP or subnet, indicative of automated credential stuffing tools. Legitimate users produce low single-digit login attempts per minute; credential stuffing tools generate dozens to hundreds, often targeting the authentication API directly rather than the web login form.

title: Geographic Impossibility Login
text: Detects login attempts from geographically impossible locations within a short timeframe. When a user authenticates from one country and a second authentication occurs from a distant country within a window that makes physical travel impossible, it strongly indicates credential compromise and concurrent use by an attacker.

title: Device Fingerprint Anomaly
text: Detects a known device fingerprint presenting with changed underlying characteristics such as OS version, screen resolution, timezone, or installed fonts. Attackers using antidetect browsers (Multilogin, GoLogin, Dolphin Anty) import stolen device fingerprints but often have mismatches in lower-level hardware attributes that this rule correlates.

title: Combo List Iteration Pattern
text: Detects sequential username patterns typical of combo list iteration during credential stuffing attacks. Attackers feed sorted credential lists into stuffing tools, producing login attempts where usernames appear in alphabetical or near-alphabetical order with minimal timing variation between attempts, a pattern never seen in organic user behavior.

title: Distributed Credential Stuffing
text: Detects low-and-slow distributed credential stuffing attacks spread across multiple source IPs to evade per-IP rate limiting. Advanced attackers use residential proxy networks and botnets to distribute attempts, making each source IP appear benign while the aggregate attack targets many accounts. This rule aggregates failed login patterns across source IPs sharing common characteristics.

title: Residential Proxy Login Attempt
text: Detects login attempts originating from known residential proxy networks. Credential stuffing actors increasingly route attacks through residential proxies (Luminati/Bright Data, Oxylabs, SmartProxy) to appear as legitimate home users and bypass IP-reputation blocklists. This rule correlates source IPs against residential proxy threat intelligence feeds.

title: Credential Spray Single Password
text: Detects password spraying attacks where a single password (or small set of passwords) is tested across many accounts. Unlike traditional credential stuffing which uses unique username-password pairs, password spraying tries common or recently breached passwords against a large account population to avoid per-account lockout thresholds.

title: Beneficiary Change Velocity Anomaly
text: Detects multiple beneficiary additions or modifications on a single account within a short time window. Rapid beneficiary changes are a strong pre-cursor to payment diversion fraud, where an attacker positions new destination accounts before initiating unauthorized wires.

title: Rapid Contact Information Change
text: Detects when email, phone number, and mailing address are all changed on an account within a short window. A full contact information swap is a hallmark of account takeover where the attacker locks out the legitimate owner before executing fraud.

title: MFA Method Switch Before High-Value Transaction
text: Detects when an account's multi-factor authentication method is changed (e.g., from hardware token to SMS or email OTP) shortly before a high-value wire or ACH transaction is initiated. Attackers downgrade MFA to a method they control prior to executing fraud.

title: Dormant Account Reactivation
text: Detects accounts with no transactional activity for 90 or more days that suddenly initiate financial transactions. Dormant accounts are frequently targeted by attackers because they are less likely to be monitored and credential compromise may go unnoticed.

title: Alert Threshold Modification
text: Detects when a user modifies their own transaction alert thresholds or disables notifications via online banking or mobile app. Attackers raise alert thresholds or suppress notifications to prevent the legitimate account holder from being alerted to unauthorized transactions.

title: Wire Beneficiary Name Mismatch
text: Detects when the wire beneficiary name provided by the originator does not match the account holder name at the receiving institution. Name mismatches on wire transfers are a strong indicator of payment diversion fraud where funds are redirected to accounts controlled by the attacker.

title: Power of Attorney or Authorized Signer Change
text: Detects changes to power of attorney designations or authorized signers on commercial and business accounts. Fraudsters may socially engineer or forge POA documents to gain control of business accounts, enabling them to initiate high-value transactions.

title: Account Type Conversion Anomaly
text: Detects suspicious account type conversions such as savings-to-checking or personal-to-business. These conversions can unlock higher transaction limits, wire capabilities, or ACH origination, which attackers exploit to move larger amounts after taking over a limited account.

title: First-Time International Wire to New Country
text: Detects international wire transfers sent to a country that has no prior transaction history for the originating account. First-time international wires, especially to high-risk corridors, are a key indicator of business email compromise and payment diversion schemes.

title: Transaction Amount Clustering Near Reporting Threshold
text: Detects transactions that cluster just below regulatory reporting thresholds ($3,000 for international transfers, $10,000 for CTR filing). Structuring transactions to evade reporting requirements is itself a federal offense and a strong indicator of money laundering or fraud monetization.

title: Split Transfer Chain Detection
text: Detects when a large inbound amount is split into multiple smaller outbound transfers to different beneficiaries in sequence. This layering technique is used to obscure the origin and destination of fraudulently obtained funds.

title: After-Hours Wire Transfer Initiation
text: Detects wire transfers initiated outside the account's established normal business hours. Attackers often execute unauthorized wires during evenings, weekends, or holidays when fraud detection staff and account holders are less likely to notice.

title: Rapid Outbound Wire After Large Inbound
text: Detects a large outbound wire or ACH transfer initiated within hours of receiving a large inbound deposit. This pass-through pattern is characteristic of compromised accounts being used as intermediary conduits in fraud or money laundering schemes.

title: Beneficiary Country Mismatch with Business Profile
text: Detects wire transfers to countries where the account holder has no established business relationship or prior transaction history. Combined with other indicators, this can reveal business email compromise where payment instructions are altered to redirect funds to attacker-controlled accounts in foreign jurisdictions.

title: Round-Dollar Wire Amount Pattern
text: Detects unusual patterns of wire transfers in round dollar amounts (e.g., $5,000, $10,000, $25,000). While individual round-amount wires are common, a pattern of multiple round-amount wires is atypical for legitimate business payments and may indicate structured or test transactions by fraudsters.

title: ACH Return Rate Anomaly
text: Detects ACH originators with an elevated return or reversal rate exceeding normal thresholds. High ACH return rates (especially R10 unauthorized, R29 corporate not authorized) may indicate the account is being used to initiate unauthorized debits against victim accounts.

title: Wire to FATF High-Risk Jurisdiction
text: Detects wire transfers to jurisdictions on the FATF high-risk or increased monitoring lists. While not inherently fraudulent, wires to these jurisdictions combined with other risk factors (new beneficiary, unusual amount, after-hours) significantly elevate the risk of money laundering or fraud monetization.

title: Payment Instruction Velocity Spike
text: Detects when multiple payment instructions (wires, ACH batches, or internal transfers) are submitted in rapid succession from a single account or user session. High-velocity payment submissions suggest automated or scripted fraud execution, often seen after credential compromise.

title: Mule Rapid ATM Withdrawal After Inbound Transfer
text: Detects cash withdrawals at ATMs occurring shortly after an inbound wire or ACH transfer. Money mules frequently convert electronically received fraud proceeds to cash as quickly as possible to prevent recovery, often hitting daily ATM limits across multiple machines.

title: Account Age vs Transaction Volume Mismatch
text: Detects accounts less than 90 days old that exhibit transaction volumes exceeding the typical profile for mature accounts. Newly opened accounts with abnormally high volume are a primary indicator of purpose-built mule accounts created specifically to funnel illicit funds.

title: Multi-Bank Funnel Pattern
text: Detects accounts receiving funds from multiple external financial institutions that are then consolidated and sent outbound to a single destination. This funnel pattern is a hallmark of money mule operations where proceeds from multiple fraud victims are aggregated before being laundered.

title: Crypto Off-Ramp After Wire or ACH Receipt
text: Detects a pattern where an account receives a wire or ACH credit and then promptly initiates a transfer to a known cryptocurrency exchange or digital asset platform. Converting fraud proceeds to cryptocurrency provides near-irreversible laundering, making this a critical monetization indicator.

title: Peer-to-Peer Transfer Chain (Smurfing Pattern)
text: Detects chains of peer-to-peer transfers across multiple accounts where funds move through a sequence of intermediary accounts (A to B to C to D). This smurfing pattern is used to layer fraud proceeds through multiple hops, making tracing difficult.

title: Mule Recruitment Test Deposit Pattern
text: Detects accounts receiving multiple small "test" deposits from many distinct external sources. Mule recruiters validate new mule accounts by sending micro-deposits from various fraud proceeds before routing larger amounts. The pattern of many small inbound transfers from unrelated senders is highly anomalous for personal accounts.

title: Rapid Fund Layering Through Shell Accounts
text: Detects rapid fund movement through multiple accounts with minimal retention time, indicative of layering through shell or pass-through accounts. Funds transit through each account within hours with near-zero balance retention, suggesting the accounts exist solely to obscure the money trail.

title: Carrier Change Authentication Correlation
text: Detects a carrier or SIM change event immediately followed by an authentication attempt on a banking platform. SIM swap attacks involve social engineering or insider compromise at a mobile carrier to port the victim's phone number to an attacker-controlled SIM, after which the attacker uses SMS-based MFA to access accounts. The tight temporal correlation between carrier change and login is the key indicator.

title: New Device High-Value Transaction
text: Detects a high-value financial transaction initiated from a new or previously unknown device shortly after initial authentication. Attackers who have compromised credentials and bypassed MFA via SIM swap typically move quickly to execute high-value transfers from a device with no prior history on the account, exploiting the narrow window before the victim notices.

title: MFA Push Bombing
text: Detects rapid repeated MFA push notifications sent to the same user, a technique known as MFA fatigue or push bombing. Attackers who have obtained valid credentials bombard the victim with push authentication requests, hoping the user will approve one out of frustration or confusion, thereby granting the attacker access.

title: SIM Swap Indicator Chain
text: Detects the full SIM swap attack chain: phone number change followed by password reset followed by high-value account action in rapid sequence. This multi-stage correlation captures the complete attack lifecycle where the attacker first takes over the phone number, then uses it to reset the account password via SMS OTP, and finally executes a high-value transfer or account modification.

title: VoIP Number MFA Enrollment
text: Detects MFA enrollment using VoIP or virtual phone numbers instead of legitimate mobile carrier numbers. Attackers who have compromised an account often enroll a disposable VoIP number (Google Voice, TextNow, Twilio) as the MFA phone to maintain persistent access and intercept future OTP codes without relying on SIM swap persistence.

title: MFA Method Downgrade
text: Detects when an account's MFA method is changed from a strong phishing-resistant factor (FIDO2/WebAuthn, hardware token, authenticator app) to a weaker method (SMS OTP, voice call). Attackers who compromise account credentials may downgrade the MFA method to one they can intercept via SIM swap or SS7 exploitation, enabling persistent account takeover.

title: Voice Biometric Confidence Score Anomaly for Known Caller
text: Detects when a voice biometric verification score for a previously enrolled caller falls below an acceptable confidence threshold, which may indicate a deepfake or voice-clone attempt impersonating a legitimate customer. Legitimate callers typically produce scores above 85; scores between 40-70 with a previously stable voiceprint warrant investigation.

title: Callback Number Mismatch for Claimed Institution
text: Detects when an inbound caller claims to represent a specific financial institution or internal department, but the originating ANI or callback number does not match the institution's known directory of outbound numbers. This is a common indicator of vishing and social engineering, especially when combined with voice-clone technology to impersonate bank officials.

title: Audio Compression Artifacts Indicative of AI-Generated Speech
text: Detects audio streams exhibiting compression artifacts, spectral anomalies, or frequency-band irregularities characteristic of AI-generated or text-to-speech synthesis engines. These include unnaturally uniform pitch contours, missing micro-pauses, absence of breath sounds, and codec artifacts from re-encoding through real-time deepfake pipelines.

title: Deepfake Anomalies in Video KYC Session
text: Detects anomalies during video KYC (Know Your Customer) sessions that may indicate the use of deepfake technology. Indicators include irregular frame rates suggesting real-time face-swapping, inconsistent lighting between face and background, lip-sync desynchronization, unnatural eye-blink patterns, and face-boundary artifacts.

title: AI-Generated Document Detection in Verification
text: Detects indicators of AI-generated or synthetically created identity documents submitted during verification workflows. Flags include metadata anomalies (missing EXIF data, uniform noise patterns), font rendering inconsistencies, micro-printing irregularities, and GAN-generated portrait artifacts such as asymmetric earrings or irregular hair boundaries.

title: Real-Time Payment to New Payee After Credential or Contact Change
text: Detects when a real-time or instant payment (Zelle, FedNow, RTP) is initiated to a previously unseen payee within 24 hours of a credential change (password reset, MFA re-enrollment) or contact information update (email, phone, address). This pattern is strongly associated with account takeover followed by immediate monetization via authorized push payment.

title: Instant Payment Velocity Spike Above 30-Day Baseline
text: Detects a sudden spike in instant payment frequency that significantly exceeds the account's established 30-day baseline. A spike is defined as the current day's instant payment count exceeding 3 standard deviations above the rolling 30-day mean, indicating potential account compromise or mule activity where the account is being drained rapidly.

title: Cross-Platform Deposit and Withdrawal Chain
text: Detects a pattern where funds are received via one payment rail (e.g., ACH, wire) and then immediately sent out via a different payment rail (e.g., Zelle, FedNow) within a short window. This cross-rail chaining is a common layering technique used to obscure the origin of funds and complicate tracing, often associated with money mule operations and authorized push payment fraud monetization.

title: Repeated A2A Payments at Maximum Per-Transaction Limit
text: Detects multiple account-to-account payments where each transaction is at or near the maximum per-transaction limit (e.g., $2,500 for Zelle, $500,000 for FedNow). Fraudsters often structure payments at the exact limit to maximize extraction speed while avoiding aggregate-amount alerts, a behavior rarely seen in legitimate consumer transactions.

title: New Account Sending Multiple Instant Payments
text: Detects accounts less than 30 days old that initiate multiple instant payments within a short time window. Newly opened accounts used for rapid instant-payment disbursement are a strong indicator of synthetic identity fraud or mule accounts created specifically for the monetization phase of a fraud scheme.

title: Zelle Recipient Enumeration via Multiple Failed Lookups
text: Detects multiple failed Zelle recipient lookups from a single account or session, which may indicate enumeration activity. Attackers probe email addresses and phone numbers to identify which are registered with Zelle before launching targeted social engineering or authorized push payment attacks against confirmed users.

title: Real-Time Payment Followed by Immediate Refund or Return Request
text: Detects a pattern where a real-time payment (RTP or FedNow) is sent and then an immediate refund, return, or Request for Return of Funds (RROF) is submitted within a short window. This pattern may indicate a double-dip fraud scheme where the sender initiates an irrevocable payment, then exploits the refund process to recover funds while the recipient also retains them.

title: Fake Tracking ID (FTID) Refund Fraud Indicators
text: Detects indicators of fake tracking ID (FTID) refund fraud, where a customer claims a package was not received or returned by providing a manipulated or fabricated tracking number. Indicators include tracking numbers that show delivery to the carrier facility but not to the customer address, tracking IDs associated with lightweight packages inconsistent with the order, or reuse of known FTID patterns across multiple refund claims.

title: Abnormally High Refund Rate Per Customer Account
text: Detects customer accounts with an abnormally high refund-to-order ratio over a rolling window. Accounts exceeding a refund rate of 40% across 10 or more orders within 90 days are flagged as potential refund abusers or participants in refunding-as-a-service (RaaS) schemes, where professional refunders exploit return policies systematically.

title: Triangulation Fraud Shipping Pattern Detection
text: Detects orders where the shipping address differs from the billing address and matches known drop-ship or reshipping patterns associated with triangulation fraud. In triangulation fraud, a fraudster lists goods on a marketplace, collects payment from a victim buyer, then purchases the item from a legitimate retailer using stolen payment credentials, shipping directly to the victim. Indicators include shipping to known drop addresses, freight forwarders, or addresses seen across multiple unrelated accounts.

title: Return Without Receipt Clustering by Customer or Region
text: Detects clusters of product returns submitted without receipts or order references from the same customer identity or geographic region. Organized return fraud rings often exploit no-receipt return policies by using stolen merchandise or purchasing items specifically for return, concentrating activity across nearby store locations or using multiple accounts linked to the same region.

title: High-Value Item Not Received Claims Exceeding Threshold
text: Detects "item not received" (INR) claims filed on high-value orders that exceed a configurable dollar threshold. High-value INR claims are a primary vector for refund fraud, particularly when the delivery confirmation shows successful delivery. Repeated INR claims on expensive items from the same account or device fingerprint are strong indicators of first-party fraud or professional refunding services.

title: Excessive Promotional Code or Coupon Abuse from Related Accounts
text: Detects excessive use of promotional codes, referral bonuses, or coupon offers from accounts that share common attributes such as device fingerprint, IP address, payment method, or shipping address. This pattern indicates promo abuse rings that create multiple accounts to exploit new-customer or referral promotions repeatedly, often using synthetic or stolen identities.

title: DPRK IT Worker Resume Geographic Mismatch
text: Detects job applicants whose resume combines a U.S. residential address with education credentials from non-North American institutions (Singapore, Japan, Hong Kong, China, South Korea). This pattern is a key DPRK IT worker indicator documented by FBI IC3 and DOJ enforcement actions. Legitimate applicants with this profile exist, but the combination with thin credit files or recently created LinkedIn profiles significantly elevates risk.

title: VPN/Proxy Login Anomaly — Astrill or Residential Proxy
text: Detects corporate VPN authentication events originating from known Astrill VPN infrastructure, residential proxy services, or connection patterns indicating VPN-over-VPN layering. DPRK IT workers route connections through Astrill VPN to U.S.-based proxy laptops before connecting to corporate infrastructure, creating a characteristic multi-hop pattern with elevated latency and IP reputation indicators.

title: Multi-Operator Behavioral Shift — Timezone and Communication Anomaly
text: Detects behavioral patterns suggesting multiple operators are sharing a single employee identity. Indicators include login activity spanning incompatible timezones within a single day, significant shifts in communication style or vocabulary between time windows, and device fingerprint changes that correlate with timezone transitions. DPRK IT workers often operate in shifts from different locations using the same stolen identity.

title: Bulk Code Repository Clone by New Employee
text: Detects a new employee (within first 14 days of onboarding) cloning or downloading multiple code repositories, especially repositories outside their assigned team or project scope. DPRK IT workers frequently begin exfiltrating source code within hours of gaining access, cloning entire organizational repositories to personal GitHub accounts or external cloud storage.

title: Credential Store Access Anomaly During Onboarding
text: Detects new employees accessing browser credential stores, password managers, API key management systems, or SSO session token stores at rates significantly above peer baselines during the first 14 days of employment. DPRK IT workers harvest credentials, session cookies, and API keys early in their tenure for exfiltration to DPRK cyber units and as leverage for post-termination extortion.

title: Salary Direct Deposit Rapid Cryptocurrency Conversion
text: Detects patterns where salary direct deposit payments are rapidly converted to cryptocurrency (USDT, USDC, BTC) within 48 hours of deposit, particularly when the receiving account was recently opened or when multiple employee accounts show the same conversion pattern through the same exchange or payment processor. DPRK IT workers convert salary to cryptocurrency for transfer to regime-controlled wallets, often using daily conversion limits to avoid AML alerts.

title: Post-Termination Data Extortion Indicator
text: Detects indicators of post-termination data extortion, where a recently terminated or resigned employee communicates ransom demands referencing specific internal proprietary code, documents, or trade secrets. DPRK IT workers have escalated to this tactic since mid-2024, threatening to publish exfiltrated source code on public repositories or sell proprietary data unless payment is made. Indicators include communication from personal channels containing references to internal systems, and the appearance of company code on public GitHub repositories created by former employee-linked accounts.
